findings.label: Nine of twelve timed workloads are dispatch-bound: device task time is 1.5-5.2 us while eval latency is 30.3-31.5 us
findings.backend_detail: msprof op_summary per-invocation Task Start Time / Task Duration columns; no host-side (Python) counters are exposed, so host cost is bounded by subtraction against eval latency

findings.inference: In the same msprof acquisition, consecutive device tasks for the small/mid workloads are separated by 39.7 us (1024 fp16) and 45.4 us (1M fp32) while the kernel itself runs 1.0-5.8 us: the vector core is idle for the large majority of each interval, so the cadence is set by the launch path, not by device work. Eval latency for the same nine workloads is 30.3-31.5 us against 11.1-12.9 us for the aten reference, i.e. our dispatch path costs roughly 18-19 us more than the reference's per call. The gap between eval latency and device duration comes from independent collections, so this is an order-of-magnitude attribution, not an exact host/device split; nevertheless device work accounts for at most ~17% of measured latency at 1M fp32 and ~5% at 1024 fp16. This regime covers 9 of the 12 timed workloads and therefore carries most of geo_mean.

findings.label: 4096x4096 fp32 is device-bound with fully serialized AIV pipes (MTE2+MTE3+VEC+scalar sum equals aiv_time)
findings.backend_detail: msprof pipe ratios are relative to aiv_time; ratios summing to ~1.0 indicate no intra-program overlap (they would exceed 1.0 with pipelining)

aiv_mte3_time(us) [ratio 0.309]
aiv_vec_time(us) [ratio 0.231]
aiv_scalar_time(us) [ratio 0.194]
same serialization on fp16 4096x4096: aiv 20.829 vs mte2 5.661 + mte3 6.387 + vec 4.711 + scalar 4.210

findings.inference: For timing-11 the four AIV pipe times sum to 41.23 us against aiv_time 40.909 us, i.e. the pipes occupy disjoint intervals and provide no overlap; the kernel is 'busy' ~98% of its duration yet the critical path is the sum of four serial stages, not the maximum. The same additive pattern holds at fp16 (20.97 us sum vs 20.83 us aiv_time). Each program in _neg_exact handles exactly one tile with no loop (main.py:44-47), so Triton has no opportunity to software-pipeline the next load against the current negate/store. If the pipes overlapped, the bound would fall to max(MTE2, MTE3, VEC) ~12.6 us for fp32 and ~6.4 us for fp16. Eval latency here (41.449 us) matches the device duration, confirming this is the one workload where device time, not dispatch, sets the score.

findings.label: 64 KiB tiles already sustain ~5.9 TB/s aggregate MTE2 read rate (L2-resident); per-program DMA width is not the residual limit
findings.backend_detail: derived logical rates from aiv_mte2_time in op_summary; logical bytes from the workload spec (4096x4096 fp32/fp16), not physical DRAM counters

evidence.metric: logical MTE2 read rate (1024 blocks x 64 KiB = 67.1 MB / aiv_mte2_time 11.168 us)
logical MTE2 read rate (512 blocks x 64 KiB = 33.5 MB / aiv_mte2_time 5.661 us)
aiv_mte3_time(us) for the store side at identical tile bytes

findings.inference: Halving the program count (1024 -> 512) halves MTE2 time exactly (11.168 -> 5.661 us) at identical 64 KiB per-program tiles, so per-program DMA cost is byte-proportional and already near the ceiling: ~5.9-6.0 TB/s aggregate read and ~5.3 TB/s write. The 67 MB fp32 tensor fits inside the 176160768-byte L2 of this device, so these are L2-resident rates, not HBM bandwidth, and must not be quoted as HBM utilization. Consequence for the frozen hypothesis: its mechanism ('larger per-program DMA bursts raise effective device bandwidth from ~0.9 TB/s toward ~5 TB/s') describes an effect that this round has already realized; the remaining device gap to the reference comes from the serialized pipe structure above, so further tile enlargement alone should not be expected to pay off.

findings.label: bf16 negation costs 3.9x the fp16 vector time at identical tile bytes, and the penalty appears at every size
findings.backend_detail: pipe time comparison at matched byte volume; confirming the lowering would require the instruction listing that this service advertises but that was not requested

evidence.metric: aiv_vec_time(us) for bfloat16 4096x4096 [ratio 0.553]

findings.inference: timing-7 and timing-3 move the same bytes (MTE2 5.661 us in both, MTE3 6.27 vs 6.39 us) yet bf16 spends 18.17 us in the vector pipe versus 4.71 us for fp16, and the bf16 vector share is 55% of aiv_time versus 23%. The same dtype penalty shows at 1M elements (1.398 us bf16 vec vs 0.725 us fp32 vec at the same element count). By elimination the difference is in how negation is lowered for bf16 (plausibly convert-to-fp32 / emulated arithmetic rather than a native 16-bit negate). This is a secondary effect: it inflates the device time of the two bf16 large/mid workloads but does not change the dispatch-bound conclusion for the nine small/mid workloads, and it cannot be resolved from counters alone.

performance_interpretation: Round 3 eval (fingerprint 2a97cc87..., geo_mean 0.41288 vs 0.28315 in round 2, +45.8%) splits the twelve timed workloads into two clearly separated regimes. Regime A, nine workloads (all shapes except 4096x4096): fp16/bf16/fp32 at 1024, 65536 and 1048576 elements. Their device kernels take 1.5-5.2 us, yet eval latency is 30.3-31.5 us, and same-acquisition task-start cadence is 39.7-45.4 us, so the vector core is idle for most of every iteration; latency is set by the per-call launch path, which costs ~18-19 us more than the aten reference's 11.1-12.9 us. These nine workloads contribute the bulk of geo_mean and are where the remaining headroom is (each could approach speedup 1.0). Regime B, three workloads (4096x4096 fp32/fp16/bf16): device time 41.8/22.0/34.2 us matches or nearly matches eval latency 41.4/30.4/34.0 us, so here device work sets the score. In this regime the four AIV pipes are serialized (their times sum to aiv_time), the 64 KiB tile already achieves ~5.9-6.0 TB/s L2-resident reads, and bf16 pays a further 3.9x vector-time penalty versus fp16. Verdict on the frozen hypothesis: the retile prediction is supported. It forecast 152 us -> 34-42 us for the large workloads with the nine host-bound ones staying at 31-36 us and geo_mean ~0.42; measured results are 30.4/34.0/41.4 us for the large ones and 30.3-31.5 us for the nine, with geo_mean 0.4129. Its stated mechanism, however, is only partially right: the gain came from fewer programs at an already near-ceiling per-program DMA rate, and the residual device time is a pipe-serialization problem rather than a bandwidth shortfall.

next_experiment.action_description: Attack Regime A only: reduce the per-call host dispatch inside run() to a single pre-bound launch. At specialization time (keyed on dtype plus the exact/tail/strided branch) precompute and cache a closure holding (compiled.run, compiled.function, packed_metadata, grid, stream, tail-arg tuple), so a steady-state call performs one dict lookup plus one launch(...) call. Hoist the device index and current-stream lookups out of the per-call path, and avoid rebuilding the tuple key and re-calling A.is_contiguous()/_device_index() where the value is already known for that specialization. Keep the 64 KiB tiling, the exact/tail/strided kernel split, in-place storage semantics, stride handling, and the existing run() body intact and reachable as a fallback. Do not change the device kernels in this experiment, so the measurement stays attributable to the host path.
next_experiment.expected_impact: If at least ~10 of the ~19 us gap to the reference is Python-side dispatch, the nine small/mid workloads move from 30.3-31.5 us to about 20-25 us, lifting geo_mean from 0.4129 toward 0.50-0.57. The three 4096x4096 workloads are device-bound and are expected to stay within noise (30.4/34.0/41.4 us), which doubles as the control that the change did not perturb device code.
next_experiment.risks_and_rollback: Risks: a cached stream or device index can go stale if the harness creates tensors on a different device/stream, and a pre-bound arg tuple can silently drop a changed argument, breaking in-place identity or strided-view semantics. Mitigation: keep the existing per-call path behind a runtime flag, add checks for same-object return, storage mutation, odd lengths (1025 tail), strided slices, NaN/Inf and 7x9 shapes before any formal eval. Rollback: revert to the round-0003 source (sha256 d50a4830...) if any of the 18 correctness workloads regresses or if no timing workload improves.
success_criteria: All 18 correctness workloads PASSED, including the five (correctness-5/11/17 and the previously non-finite cases) that must keep the NaN/Inf and strided semantics correct; in-place identity and storage mutation still hold.
Each of the nine Regime-A timing workloads at or below 28 us (from 30.3-31.5 us), and headline geo_mean at or above 0.45 versus 0.4129 now.
The three 4096x4096 controls stay within +/-5% of 30.36 / 34.02 / 41.45 us, confirming device code was untouched.

Falsification branch: if the nine workloads remain at or above 29.5 us, treat 'the remainder is Python dispatch in run()' as disproven and move to the device-side pipe-overlap experiment (loop over multiple tiles per program so Triton can pipeline MTE2/VEC/MTE3, whose serialized sum is the critical path in Regime B).

warnings: msprof timing is diagnostic and never replaces eval latency; eval speedups above come only from get_profile_context.

msprof exposes no host-side (Python/C-launcher) counters, so the ~25-29 us non-device portion on Regime A is inferred by comparing device task duration against eval latency from independent collections, not measured as a split.
The 4096x4096 tensors (33.5-67.1 MB) fit within the device's 176160768-byte L2, so the derived ~5.9 TB/s rates are L2-resident logical rates and must not be reported as HBM bandwidth or saturation.
Per-block pipe ratios are relative to aiv_time and pipelines can overlap; the conclusion for Regime B rests on the pipe times summing to aiv_time, not on any single high percentage.
The bf16 vector-time penalty is identified by counter comparison only; confirming an fp32 emulation path would require the instruction-listing capability that was not requested this round.
open_questions: How much of the ~18-19 us gap to the aten reference on Regime A is Python code inside run() versus the Triton launcher's C-side binding versus the harness iteration floor? A bounded host-side diagnostic (CPU timing of the launch path, outside formal eval) would separate these.

Would a loop-over-tiles kernel (K tiles per program, e.g. 4-8 iterations per program) let Triton software-pipeline MTE2/VEC/MTE3 in Regime B and bring fp32 4096x4096 from 41.8 us toward the ~12.6 us max-pipe bound, and does the same change alter Regime A?
Is the bf16 18.17 us vector time due to convert-to-fp32 emulation, and would a 16-bit-native negate or a different element type path reduce timing-7 below 34.0 us?
